nameStory: The skunk currant earned its memorable name from the strong, musky odor it releases when you brush against its leaves or crush them between your fingers. This pungent smell is surprisingly similar to the spray of its mammalian namesake, making it one of the most unforgettable shrubs you'll encounter on a woodland hike!
description: Skunk currant is a low-growing deciduous shrub that typically reaches 2-4 feet tall and spreads by underground runners to form small colonies. It belongs to the same family as garden gooseberries and currants, producing small clusters of tiny flowers in spring followed by red berries in summer. The plant has distinctive maple-like leaves and thrives in the cool, moist forests of northern New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Hand-shaped leaves with 3-5 deep lobes, similar to a small maple leaf but with a soft, almost velvety texture and prominent veins underneath

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-white or pinkish flowers hang in drooping clusters of 6-15 blooms, each flower smaller than a pencil eraser with 5 petals

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red berries covered with tiny glands that make them feel slightly sticky to the touch, ripening in mid to late summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling shrub that rarely exceeds 4 feet tall, often forming patches through underground spreading

idTips.label: Distinctive Odor
idTips.description: Crushing or bruising any part of the plant releases a strong, skunk-like musky smell that's unmistakable once you've experienced it

habitat: Skunk currant thrives in cool, moist woods throughout northern New England, particularly in areas with rich, organic soil. You'll often find it in mixed coniferous-deciduous forests, along shaded stream banks, and in mountain valleys where the soil stays consistently damp. It's especially common in areas that receive filtered sunlight under a partial forest canopy.

seasonality.spring: Small clusters of greenish-white flowers appear in late spring, usually May to early June. New leaves emerge with a fresh green color and soft texture.
seasonality.summer: Red berries ripen from July through August, and the distinctive musky odor is strongest when leaves are crushed. Foliage remains green and full.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow or reddish before dropping, though fall color is usually subtle. Berries may persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare twigs show a reddish-brown color with small buds. The shrub's low, spreading growth pattern becomes more visible without leaves.

funFact: Despite its off-putting smell, skunk currant berries are actually edible and were traditionally used by Indigenous peoples to make jellies and sauces, though most people today find the musky flavor too strong for their taste!
confusionNotes: Skunk currant's maple-like leaves might fool you into thinking it's a young maple tree, but the key difference is that currant leaves grow alternately on the stem while maple leaves grow in opposite pairs. Plus, crushing a currant leaf will immediately reveal that unmistakable skunky smell!
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that currants and gooseberries belong to the same plant family and were once banned in some areas because they can host a disease that affects pine trees. The ban has been lifted in most places, but it explains why these native shrubs are less familiar to many people today.
compareHints: Among New England's currants and gooseberries, skunk currant is unique for its strong musky odor and preference for cooler, northern forests. Unlike prickly gooseberry which has thorns, or red currant with its more upright growth, skunk currant stays low and sprawling. The glandular, sticky berries also help distinguish it from smooth-fruited relatives like American black currant.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Ribes species, prickly gooseberry is the most heavily armed with spines, making it easy to distinguish from the spineless currants like red currant or American black currant.
Unlike its gooseberry relatives in the Ribes genus, red currant has completely smooth, thornless stems and bears its fruit in long drooping clusters rather than scattered individual berries.
Among New England's Ribes species, swamp currant stands out for its incredibly dense coat of small prickles - no other currant or gooseberry in the region is quite so thoroughly armored.

Among its Ribes relatives, smooth gooseberry is distinguished by having fewer thorns than prickly gooseberry but more than the currants, and its berries grow individually rather than in the long clusters typical of red and black currants.
Among New England's Ribes species, American black currant is distinguished by its strong musky leaf scent and completely smooth stems.
Unlike its spiny gooseberry relatives in the Ribes family, northern redcurrant is completely thornless and has a sprawling rather than upright growth habit.
European gooseberry has much more prominent three-pronged spines than our native prickly gooseberry or smooth gooseberry.
Appalachian gooseberry stands out from other Ribes species by its sweet berries and relatively smooth stems - unlike the very thorny prickly gooseberry or the skunky-smelling skunk currant.
Among the Ribes family, blackcurrant stands out for lacking thorns (unlike most gooseberries) and having that distinctive strong musky leaf scent.

Golden currant stands out among New England's Ribes species with its bright yellow flowers and sweet fragrance, while most relatives like skunk currant and American black currant have small, greenish or whitish flowers.
